analysis.one_liner: Required tighter inspections, community grants, and new-facility bans in counties with the heaviest toxic pollution.
analysis.headline: The bill gathered 44 cosponsors and held subcommittee hearings but never received a markup or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the government to rank the 100 counties carrying the heaviest toxic chemical loads, inspect every toxic chemical facility in those areas at least every two years, and pay for community groups to get technical help tracking pollution. If a federal health study found that residents were being harmed, the President would have to propose new rules, and new polluting facilities could be barred from those areas until health-based standards were met.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of the 100 counties designated as Environmental High Impact Areas — typically communities carrying the heaviest concentration of toxic facilities — would gain mandatory facility inspections, federal funding to hire technical experts, direct disclosure of chemical releases and health effects, and a pause on new polluting facilities if a federal health study confirmed harm.

how_it_helps.text: The bill required compliance inspections or reviews of all toxic chemical facilities in designated high-impact areas within two years of enactment and at least every two years thereafter [S2].

It authorized grants of up to $50,000 so residents of affected areas could obtain technical assistance with inspections, reviews, and health studies, funded by fees on the toxic chemical facilities themselves rather than general appropriations [S2].

It required a federal health study comparing cancer, birth defects, infant mortality, and respiratory disease rates in high-impact counties to other counties, with results delivered directly to affected communities and tribal governments [S2].

If the health study found significant harm, the President would have to propose legislation to close regulatory loopholes, expand right-to-know reporting, and impose taxes or restrictions on emissions, and new toxic facilities could be barred from those areas until health-based levels were attained [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Toxic chemical facilities in designated high-impact counties: they would bear new fees funding community grants, mandatory inspections, potentially higher emission taxes, and a moratorium on siting or permitting new polluting facilities until health standards were met.
analysis.who_pays_short: Toxic chemical facilities in those counties

drawbacks.text: The bill's mechanism keyed designations to total weight of toxic chemicals present in a county, an approach critics could argue tracks tonnage rather than actual exposure and risk; the bill itself acknowledged this by requiring the Administrator to adjust for relative toxicity and exposure with the best available data [S3].

Facility owners would face new fees, inspection costs, and potential restrictions on siting and permitting; a facility could be barred from operating in an affected area until health-based levels were attained, which industry groups characterized as a construction and expansion freeze [S2].

The community grant program required grant recipients to contribute 20 percent of the grant cost unless they demonstrated financial need, limiting access for the lowest-income groups it targeted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of the most heavily polluted counties, the bill offered concrete, verifiable benefits: more inspections, funding for expert help, and honest data on local health effects, all funded by fees on the facilities themselves rather than taxpayers. The main cost falls on chemical and waste facilities in those counties, which is the point of the bill. Weaknesses are in design rather than intent: ranking counties by chemical tonnage is a crude exposure measure, and the 20 percent local match could exclude some of the poorest communities.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees and reached subcommittee hearings in November 1993, but no committee ever voted to advance it and the full House never took it up before Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. John Lewis (D-GA) introduced the Environmental Justice Act of 1992 on May 12, 1993, joined by 24 original cosponsors [S3].

The bill was referred jointly to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Public Works and Transportation, Education and Labor, and Agriculture — and then divided among five subcommittees in May and June 1993 [S5].
It attracted 44 cosponsors, 42 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican, and additional sponsors added in December 1993 [S4].
Two days of subcommittee hearings were held on November 17-18, 1993, but no committee reported the bill and no floor vote ever occurred before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of toxic chemical facilities in heavily polluted counties were better off, since the mandatory inspections, fees, disclosure requirements, and possible siting moratorium never took effect. Communities in those counties remained without the federal health study and enforcement tools the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Polluting facility operators; communities got nothing

industries.industry: Toxic chemical and hazardous waste facilities
industries.note: The bill imposed inspections at least every two years, fees to fund community grants, possible emission taxes, and a moratorium on new facility siting in the 100 most heavily loaded counties. Its costs fall on these operators; its benefits flow to nearby residents [S2].

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and industrial polluters broadly
industries.note: The bill would have expanded right-to-know reporting, closed waste-regulation loopholes, and allowed restrictions on releases even where facilities were in compliance with existing law, raising operating costs in high-impact areas [S2].
